methodological_rigor.justification: The design is appropriate: two independent external validation cohorts (DFCI n=1759, TNM-I n=339) plus a TCGA technical-reproduction check for two previously published open-source EGFR prediction models. The authors use bootstrap-based 95% CIs (1000 resamples) for AUCs and include a thoughtful prevalence-matched subsampling analysis to address whether higher EGFR prevalence in the Asian subgroup explains the AUC drop. However, no formal statistical test (e.g., DeLong) is reported for AUC comparisons between ancestries, sites, or models; no sample-size/power calculation is provided for the subgroup analyses (Asian n=95, African n=54 are modest); and multiplicity across the many subgroup/threshold/site comparisons is not addressed. Handling of missing data and inter-reader/scanner variability are not described in the main text.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an external validation of a multivariable AI prediction model in independent cohorts, mapping to Oxford LoE 2b (individual cohort/validation study). The clinical question is highly relevant: EGFR genotyping gates first-line targeted therapy in LUAD, and the IASLC global survey cited shows real-world testing bottlenecks. The dual-threshold triage demonstrates a plausible near-term clinical workflow (57% reduction in rapid molecular testing with sensitivity 0.84, specificity 0.99), and the ancestry-stratified underperformance in Asian patients has direct implications for equitable deployment. The endpoint remains a surrogate (AUC, not patient outcomes), and prospective clinical utility is not demonstrated.

reporting_quality.justification: TRIPOD-AI is explicitly declared as the reporting guideline, which is appropriate for a prediction-model validation study. Key TRIPOD items are addressed in the main text (participants, predictors via published pipelines, outcome definition, performance metrics with CIs, subgroup analyses), but many methodological details are deferred to eMethods/Supplement 1 which cannot be assessed here; inclusion/exclusion criteria, missing-data handling, calibration, and detailed slide-processing QC are not visible in the main manuscript. Reproducibility posture is moderate: both evaluated models (EAGLE, DeepGEM) are open-source and TCGA is public, enabling partial external replication, but no code repository, model-weight DOI, or deposited DFCI/TNM-I derived scores are referenced in the main text.

novelty_literature.justification: The novelty is empirical/population-oriented rather than conceptual or methodological: the authors do not develop a new model but perform a rigorous head-to-head external validation of two previously published open-source EGFR-prediction models (EAGLE and DeepGEM) and extend prior work by stratifying by genetically inferred ancestry and anatomic specimen site. The ancestry-stratified underperformance in Asian patients and the pleural-site drop are genuinely useful additions and align with the demographic-bias literature cited (Vaidya et al., 2024). However, cross-cohort validation of pathology foundation models and demographic bias in computational pathology are already active areas, limiting the finding to a meaningful but incremental extension.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written in the JAMA-style structured abstract/question-findings-meaning format, with a logical flow from technical reproduction to primary cohort, external cohort, ancestry stratification, specimen site, thresholding, and triage. Numeric claims in results align with the abstract (AUCs, CIs, triage sensitivity/specificity), and figure captions for Figures 1-2 are self-contained. The Limitations section is unusually brief—only one sentence—and does not acknowledge the modest Asian subgroup size, lack of formal AUC comparison tests, or scanner/stain variability; the Conclusions section partly rehashes results rather than situating implications.

key_strengths: Large, independent two-cohort external validation (DFCI n=1759, TNM-I n=339) with a TCGA technical-reproduction anchor, directly addressing a known generalizability gap for open-source EGFR prediction models
Head-to-head benchmarking of EAGLE vs DeepGEM under identical preprocessing shows a reproducible performance gap favoring fine-tuned foundation-model adaptation over frozen features
Clinically actionable triage analysis demonstrates 57% reduction in rapid EGFR testing at sensitivity 0.84 / specificity 0.99 using a dual-threshold strategy
Ancestry-stratified analysis with genome-derived ancestry inference and a prevalence-matched subsampling control strengthens the fairness/robustness claim
Explicit TRIPOD-AI adherence and bootstrap-based 95% CIs throughout
key_concerns: No formal statistical test (e.g., DeLong) for AUC differences between models, ancestry subgroups, or specimen sites; multiplicity across many subgroup comparisons is unaddressed
Ancestry subgroups are modest (Asian n=95, African n=54, American n=101) and ancestry data are available in only one cohort, limiting generalizability of the central equity finding
Limitations section is a single sentence and does not acknowledge subgroup sample-size constraints, scanner/stain variability, lack of calibration analysis, or absence of prospective clinical utility
Main text does not reference a public code or model-score repository, and key methodological details (QC, missing data, calibration) are deferred to a supplement not available for this review
Novelty is incremental: a thorough external validation and demographic stress-test rather than a new model or new mechanistic insight
chief_reviewer.rationale: A methodologically solid, clinically relevant external validation with an important equity signal and a usable triage workflow; the paucity of inferential testing between AUCs and the thin limitations section hold it back from a tier-1 flagship but are addressable in minor revisions at a strong oncology or oncology-AI venue.
